Never Letting Go

The chained task changes grasp by opening the hand completely and trusting a free-standing cylinder to wait where it was put. It waits because it is a cylinder on its end face on a level floor. Here the hand keeps hold instead — one finger at a time, through the handover and through every turn — and the assumption is replaced by a load.

366 rollouts · rv05_manual_stored · MuJoCo 3.6 · CPU
0.4%of the task with no pad on the tool (was 49%)
52%of the shipped chain's turn rate
5/6seeds at a 30° lateral load, in the seat
11.0 mmper cycle it slips with no floor at all

What the chain was assuming

free_frac · the share of the task after set-down with nothing touching the tool

The chained task published last week gets from the carry's grasp to the gait's the simplest way there is: open the hand, fly the palm to the pose the gait study validated, close again on a ring. It works on every seed, and the reason it works is a property of the object, not of the hand. A 100×25 mm cylinder standing on its end face is statically stable out to atan(12.5/50) = 14.0°, so it simply waits.

How much waiting the chain asks for is measurable, and it is not a detail. Sampling contact at the control rate from the moment the tool is set down to the end of the gait, 49% of that window has no pad on the tool at all — the full release during the re-index, and then, every cycle, the three-pad release the gait needs to advance its contacts. For half the task the hand is not holding the thing it is manipulating.

That is fine for a cylinder on a level floor and false for almost anything else: a tool seated in a countersink and tipped a few degrees, a bench that is not level, a cable, a heavier tool, a nudge. So the question this page asks is narrow. Can the same task be run without ever letting go, and what does it cost?

The two candidate answers

Either transition from the reorientation grasp to a gaiting grasp while keeping enough contact to support the tool, or never take a gaiting grasp at all and gait from the reorientation grasp. They turn out to be the same mechanism — a handover is a relay whose target ring moved — and, more usefully, they turn out to be a matched pair: doing one without the other is worse than doing neither.

The two that fail are worth more than the two that work, because each fails for a reason that was already in the repertoire under another name.

A joint-space regrasp sweeps the pad through the tool

The obvious per-finger handover ramps one finger's joints from its carry pose to its ring pose while the other two hold. It knocks the tool over on every seed and every fraction of the wrist move tried. The carry's station and the ring's station straddle the shaft, so the straight line between them in joint space passes through the material: the tool leaves before the finger arrives. This is the same defect as the mid-air ring regrasp that fails 6/6 in the chain study, which was read there as a mid-air problem — it is not, it is a path problem, and it is present on the floor too. The fix is to plan the move in the tool's own cylindrical coordinates: retract radially at the station already held, travel to the new station and azimuth out there, close back in. Three legs, never inside the surface.

The fingers cannot absorb the wrist move

The gait's ring is only cleanly reachable from the gait's palm pose, and the carry leaves the palm 27.7 mm and 9.2° away from it: that ring's worst IK residual is 0.21 mm solved from the gait's pose and 7.6 mm solved from where the carry parks the palm. So track flies the palm there with every pad pinned to the world point it currently holds, which would move the wrist without moving the tool. This hand cannot do it: the pins run 15.8 mm short at full travel, the pads come off, and the tool is free-standing again anyway. Dragging the pads along the tool instead (slide) is worse — a loaded pad cannot be slid axially without carrying the object with it, so the tool is lifted off the floor and topples.

Neither failure is a tuning problem. Together they say the wrist move has to be given up, and that is the trade the working mode makes: the relay keeps every contact and pays for it by taking its ring at the height the pads are already at, which it reaches to 5.09 mm rather than 0.21.

The variable was worth sweeping because the answer could have been a knee. It is not — there is no fraction at which the pins hold and the ring is reachable, and the best cell in the sweep is 1/6.

The relay, and why the gait has to relay too

handover schedule × gait schedule · 6 seeds each

The working handover walks one pad at a time from the carry's stations onto the gait's ring, around the tool rather than through it, with the palm parked where the carry left it. Two pads are loaded at every instant of the transition. The gait then runs its own relay: release, return and regrasp one finger at a time instead of all three, which is the schedule probe_real_v1_gait.py has carried as --relay since the gait study and which that study measured only with the floor underneath.

handovergait releaseok no contactdeg/cycledrift mm
releaseall three together6/649.2%44.30.29
releaseone finger at a time6/617.6%29.40.35
relayall three together2/619.1%64.824.42
relayone finger at a time6/60.4%23.00.12

The two halves are a matched pair and the cross terms are worse than either diagonal. A relay handover followed by a synchronous gait is the worst cell in the study that is not an outright failure: it hands a carefully preserved grasp to a schedule that throws it away three pads at a time, 2/6. Run together, they complete every seed with 0.4% of the task uncontacted — against 49% — and 0.03 mm of lateral drift.

The cost is 23.0° per cycle against 44.3°, or 52% of the turn rate, and it is paid twice over: once because the relay's ring is the one it can reach rather than the one the gait wants, and once because two stance fingers driving while a third recovers is a smaller effective stroke than three. Over 40 cycles that is 2.50 turns against 5.08. It is also markedly more repeatable — sd 0.010 turns over three seeds against 0.081 — which is what one would expect from a primitive that never re-establishes a grasp from scratch.

Gaiting from the carry's grasp, without a handover at all

The other candidate — skip the ring, gait from whatever the carry left — is 3/6 with a synchronous release and 4/6 with a relay, at 16.5°/cycle. It still opens all three fingers together to reach its ring, so it is not actually a continuous-contact mode (17% uncontacted), and its carry-inherited grasp is not a tripod. Worth knowing it half-works; not worth preferring.

Arrival order cannot set a grip

one commanded squeeze, once all three pads are on the ring

A relay lands each pad on the ring nominally 2 mm inside the surface, which on a position servo is 2 mm of grip. It is not, because the tool moves as each finger arrives: measured across one handover the pad forces went 7.6 → 4.9 → 0.3 N, the first pad relieved by the time the third landed. The grasp has to be set explicitly afterwards, with one relative squeeze computed from the commanded pose — measuring from the achieved pose hands back exactly the deflection carrying the load, which is the bench's achieved_fraction error and cost this program 18.4 N of grip over seven reissues of a constant command.

What continuous contact buys, and what it does not

a steady lateral load on the tool, as the table tilt that would produce it

With the assumption named, it can be replaced. --tilt-deg applies a steady horizontal load of tan(θ) of the tool's own weight from the moment it is standing — what a bench out of level by θ delivers, or a cable, or a nudge that does not go away. The free-standing prediction is exact and worth stating before the sweep: a cylinder on its end face topples when tan(θ) > r/half, i.e. at 14.0°.

On a plane, never letting go buys nothing. That is the result I did not expect and it is worth being plain about: the relay fails at the same load the release chain fails at. The reason is visible in the ground-force trace — the relay's grip is what holds the tool upright, and a grip strong enough to do that also unloads the floor (69% of the window has ground contact, against 99%), removing exactly the restoring moment the 14° figure is computed from. Three pads on a 21 mm ring are a worse stabiliser than a 12.5 mm foot on a floor.

In the seat, it buys everything. The countersink stops the tool translating, so the only thing left to resist is rotation about the seated tip — and that is what a hand that has not let go is good at. The relay is 5/6 at 30°, a load of 0.58 of the tool's weight, at 19.0°/cycle against 18.5° unloaded: the load does not cost it anything measurable. The release chain is 0/6 by 16°. Neither the seat nor the grasp is sufficient alone; the pair is.

With no floor at all

handoverfloorokno contact slip mm/cycleend tilt
releasepresent6/649.2%-0.00.7

relaypresent6/60.4%-0.33.3

Deleting the floor once the grasp is established is the gait study's degenerate control, and it separates the two modes completely even though both score 0/6. The release chain drops the tool: 70% of the window uncontacted. The relay does not — 1.4% uncontacted, three pads and 20 N for all six cycles, tilt under 9° — it holds the tool and lowers it, 11.0 mm per cycle, still turning it at 8°/cycle on the way down. The gate cannot tell those apart and reports both as failures; the defect is axial slip through the grasp, not loss of grasp. That is the first floor-free gait in this program that does not end with the tool on the ground, and the thing that would close it is a term nothing currently measures.

Where this leaves the task

The chained task now has two settings rather than one, and which is right depends on what is under the tool. On a flat surface with nothing disturbing it, release and retake: it is twice as fast and the floor is genuinely doing the work. Anywhere the tool cannot be trusted to stay put — and a fastener in a seat is exactly that case — relay both the handover and the gait, at 52% of the turn rate, and the load stops mattering.

What has not been done. None of this has been through the export, trajectory-clearance or servo-limit gates — the relay's Cartesian legs are a new path shape and three of four plans that reached the control station once failed exactly that check. There is still no torsional load on the seat, so this remains a 0.0072 N·m primitive and not a fastener. The relay's grip is set once and never corrected, which is the obvious place for the first closed loop, and gaiting remains the only task in this program whose controlled variable the bench's AprilTag rig measures directly. And the axial slip that ends the floor-free run has no reward term, no scorecard entry and no design metric, on either topology that has shown it.
